children.name: Paleo-Indian Period (~15,000–8,000 BCE)
children.notes: First peoples cross Beringia land bridge from Asia; spread throughout the Americas hunting megafauna such as mammoths and giant bison.

children.name: Clovis Culture (~13,000 BCE)
children.notes: Characterized by distinctive fluted stone projectile points; considered one of the earliest widespread cultures in North America.

children.name: Folsom Culture (~10,000 BCE)
children.notes: Succeeded Clovis; specialized in hunting bison after megafauna extinction.

children.name: Archaic Period (~8,000–1,000 BCE)
children.notes: Shift toward diverse subsistence strategies — hunting smaller game, fishing, and gathering plants as the climate warmed.

children.name: Middle Archaic (~6,000–3,000 BCE)
children.notes: Evidence of semi-permanent settlements and trade networks.

children.name: Late Archaic (~3,000–1,000 BCE)
children.notes: Emergence of horticulture; construction of shell middens and early mound sites.

children.name: Adena Culture (~1,000–100 BCE)
children.notes: Built large burial mounds in the Ohio Valley; known for elaborate funerary practices and trade goods.

children.name: Hopewell Culture (~100 BCE–500 CE)
children.notes: Sophisticated trade network spanning much of North America; monumental earthworks and rich burial goods.

children.name: Introduction of Maize Agriculture (~200 CE)
children.notes: Maize cultivation spreads northward from Mesoamerica, transforming subsistence patterns.

children.name: Mississippian Culture (~800–1600 CE)
children.notes: Maize-based chiefdoms centered on large platform mounds; extensive trade and political networks.

children.name: Cahokia (~1050–1350 CE)
children.notes: Largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico, near present-day St. Louis; population estimated at 10,000–20,000.

children.name: Moundville (Alabama)
children.notes: Second largest Mississippian center; major ceremonial hub.

children.name: Ancestral Puebloans (~100–1300 CE)
children.notes: Built multi-story stone and adobe structures in the Four Corners region.

children.name: Chaco Canyon (~850–1150 CE)
children.notes: Regional center with great houses, roads, and astronomical alignments.

children.name: Mesa Verde (~600–1300 CE)
children.notes: Cliff dwellings constructed in canyon alcoves; abandoned around 1300 CE, possibly due to drought.

children.name: Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy)
children.notes: Alliance of five (later six) nations — Mohawk, Onondaga, Cayuga, Oneida, Seneca, and later Tuscarora; governed by the Great Law of Peace, which some historians argue influenced the U.S. Constitution.

children.name: Algonquian-speaking peoples
children.notes: Diverse nations including the Powhatan Confederacy, Wampanoag, Lenape, and Abenaki; inhabited the Atlantic seaboard.

children.name: Pre-horse Plains cultures
children.notes: Mostly semi-sedentary river valley farmers and bison hunters on foot before European horses transformed Plains life.

children.name: Adoption of the horse (~1680 CE)
children.notes: Horses escaped or were traded from Spanish settlements; revolutionized Plains hunting and warfare.

children.name: Pacific Northwest Peoples
children.notes: Abundant salmon runs supported complex, stratified societies without agriculture.

children.name: Leif Erikson reaches Vinland (~1000 CE)
children.notes: Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland — the only confirmed pre-Columbian European site in the Americas.

children.name: Christopher Columbus (1492)
children.notes: Sailing for Spain, Columbus lands in the Bahamas on October 12, 1492, initiating sustained contact between Europe and the Americas.

children.name: Treaty of Tordesillas (1494)
children.notes: Divided the non-European world between Spain and Portugal along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands.

children.name: Juan Ponce de León (1513)
children.notes: First European to reach mainland North America (Florida) while searching for the Fountain of Youth.

children.name: Hernán Cortés conquers Aztec Empire (1519–1521)
children.notes: Fall of Tenochtitlán opens Central America to Spanish colonization and fuels further North American exploration.

children.name: Hernando de Soto (1539–1542)
children.notes: Led the first major European expedition into the interior Southeast; his army spreads devastating disease among Native populations.

children.name: Francisco Vásquez de Coronado (1540–1542)
children.notes: Explored the American Southwest and Great Plains searching for the legendary Seven Cities of Gold.

children.name: St. Augustine founded (1565)
children.notes: Oldest continuously occupied European settlement in the present-day United States, established by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés.

children.name: Giovanni da Verrazzano (1524)
children.notes: Sailing for France, explored the Atlantic coast from the Carolinas to Newfoundland.

children.name: Jacques Cartier (1534–1542)
children.notes: Explored the St. Lawrence River; claimed Canada for France.

children.name: Samuel de Champlain founds Quebec (1608)
children.notes: Established France's most important colonial foothold in North America.

children.name: Robert La Salle reaches mouth of Mississippi (1682)
children.notes: Claimed the entire Mississippi River basin for France, naming it Louisiana.

children.name: John Cabot (1497)
children.notes: Sailing for England, Cabot reached Newfoundland or Nova Scotia, establishing England's claim to North America.

children.name: Martin Frobisher (1576–1578)
children.notes: Sought a Northwest Passage; explored Baffin Island.

children.name: Sir Francis Drake circumnavigates the globe (1577–1580)
children.notes: Plunders Spanish shipping and claims Nova Albion (California) for England.

children.name: Roanoke Colony (1585–1590)
children.notes: England's first attempt at permanent settlement in North America; the 'Lost Colony' disappeared with no definitive explanation.

children.name: Henry Hudson (1609)
children.notes: Sailing for the Dutch East India Company, Hudson explored the river bearing his name; his voyage led to Dutch settlement of New Netherland.

children.name: Columbian Exchange
children.notes: Massive transfer of plants, animals, culture, human populations, and disease between the Americas and the Old World following Columbus's voyages.

children.name: Old World to New World
children.notes: Horses, cattle, pigs, sheep, wheat, sugarcane, smallpox, measles, influenza.

children.name: New World to Old World
children.notes: Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, tobacco, cacao, syphilis (debated).

children.name: Demographic catastrophe
children.notes: European diseases killed an estimated 50–90% of indigenous populations within a century of contact.

children.name: Encomienda system
children.notes: Granted conquistadors the labor of indigenous peoples; backbone of early Spanish colonial economy.

children.name: New Mexico colony (1598)
children.notes: Juan de Oñate establishes Spanish presence in the Rio Grande valley.

children.name: Pueblo Revolt (1680)
children.notes: Pueblo peoples under Popé drive Spanish settlers out of New Mexico; Spain reconquers the region in 1692.

children.name: Spanish missions in California (1769)
children.notes: Franciscan friars, led by Junípero Serra, establish a chain of missions along the California coast.

children.name: New France
children.notes: Fur-trading empire stretching from Quebec through the Great Lakes and down the Mississippi; relied heavily on alliances with Native peoples.

children.name: Virginia (1607)
children.notes: Jamestown — first permanent English settlement. Tobacco becomes the cash crop. House of Burgesses (1619) is the first representative assembly in the Americas.

children.name: Maryland (1634)
children.notes: Founded by Cecil Calvert as a refuge for English Catholics; Maryland Toleration Act (1649) grants religious tolerance.

children.name: Carolina (1663)
children.notes: Royal charter granted; splits into North and South Carolina in 1712.

children.name: Georgia (1732)
children.notes: Last of the original thirteen colonies; founded by James Oglethorpe as a buffer against Spanish Florida and a haven for debtors.

children.name: Plymouth Colony (1620)
children.notes: Pilgrim Separatists arrive on the Mayflower; Mayflower Compact is an early self-governance document. Plymouth eventually absorbed into Massachusetts Bay in 1691.

children.name: Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630)
children.notes: Puritan migration led by John Winthrop ('City upon a Hill'); strict theocratic governance.

children.name: Rhode Island (1636)
children.notes: Founded by Roger Williams after banishment from Massachusetts; first colony to guarantee religious freedom.

children.name: Connecticut (1636)
children.notes: Founded by Thomas Hooker; Fundamental Orders (1639) often cited as first written constitution in the colonies.

children.name: New York (1664)
children.notes: England seizes New Netherland from the Dutch; renamed for the Duke of York.

children.name: Pennsylvania (1681)
children.notes: Founded by William Penn as a Quaker haven; Philadelphia becomes the largest colonial city.

children.name: Delaware (1704)
children.notes: Separated from Pennsylvania; granted own assembly.

children.name: Headright system
children.notes: Offered land grants to those who paid passage for indentured servants; fueled immigration but concentrated land ownership.

children.name: Indentured servitude
children.notes: Dominant labor system in early Virginia and Maryland; servants worked 4–7 years to pay off passage.

children.name: Introduction of enslaved Africans (1619)
children.notes: First Africans arrive in Virginia; chattel slavery gradually institutionalized through the 17th century.

children.name: Triangular Trade
children.notes: Linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas: manufactured goods to Africa, enslaved people to the Americas, raw materials back to Europe.

children.name: Navigation Acts (1651–1696)
children.notes: British mercantilist laws restricting colonial trade to British ships; sow seeds of colonial resentment.

children.name: Pequot War (1636–1638)
children.notes: English colonists and Narragansett allies destroy the Pequot nation; opens Connecticut Valley to settlement.

children.name: King Philip's War (1675–1676)
children.notes: Wampanoag leader Metacom (King Philip) leads a broad Native coalition against New England colonists; one of the deadliest colonial wars relative to population.

children.name: Bacon's Rebellion (1676)
children.notes: Nathaniel Bacon leads frontier planters and discontented servants against Virginia's governor; alarmed elites accelerate shift from indentured servitude to race-based slavery.

children.name: Salem Witch Trials (1692)
children.notes: Mass hysteria leads to the execution of 20 people in Salem, Massachusetts; later seen as a cautionary tale about theocracy and mob justice.

children.name: Queen Anne's War (1702–1713)
children.notes: North American theater of the War of the Spanish Succession; Britain gains Acadia (Nova Scotia) and Newfoundland.

children.name: French and Indian War (1754–1763)
children.notes: North American theater of the Seven Years' War; Britain defeats France and gains Canada and all territory east of the Mississippi.

children.name: Washington's early defeat at Fort Necessity (1754)
Treaty of Paris (1763)
children.notes: France cedes Canada and Louisiana east of the Mississippi to Britain; Spain cedes Florida.

children.name: Harvard College founded (1636)
children.notes: First institution of higher learning in British North America; originally trained Puritan ministers.

children.name: The Great Awakening (~1730s–1740s)
children.notes: Religious revival movement led by George Whitefield and Jonathan Edwards; challenged established churches and encouraged individual spiritual experience, inadvertently fostering democratic ideals.

children.name: Benjamin Franklin's experiments and publications
children.notes: Poor Richard's Almanack (1732), electricity experiments (1750s); embodied Enlightenment ideals of reason and self-improvement.

children.name: Enlightenment influence
children.notes: Ideas of Locke, Montesquieu, and Rousseau circulate among colonial elites; natural rights philosophy underpins later revolutionary arguments.

children.name: Proclamation of 1763
children.notes: Britain bars colonists from settling west of the Appalachians to pacify Native allies; widely ignored and resented.

children.name: Stamp Act (1765)
children.notes: First direct tax on colonists; triggers 'no taxation without representation' protests and the Stamp Act Congress.

children.name: Townshend Acts (1767)
children.notes: Taxes on imported goods; colonial boycotts follow.

children.name: Boston Massacre (1770)
children.notes: British soldiers kill five colonists during a confrontation; Paul Revere's engraving turns it into a propaganda coup.

children.name: Boston Tea Party (1773)
children.notes: Sons of Liberty dump 342 chests of British East India Company tea into Boston Harbor to protest the Tea Act.

children.name: Intolerable Acts / Coercive Acts (1774)
children.notes: Britain's punitive response to the Tea Party; closes Boston Harbor, revokes Massachusetts charter, and mandates quartering of troops.

children.name: First Continental Congress (1774)
children.notes: Delegates from twelve colonies meet in Philadelphia; agree to boycott British goods and petition the king.

children.name: Battles of Lexington and Concord (April 1775)
children.notes: 'The shot heard round the world'; open armed conflict begins between colonial militias and British regulars.

children.name: Second Continental Congress convenes (May 1775)
children.notes: Assumes governance of the colonies; establishes the Continental Army and appoints George Washington as commander.

children.name: Common Sense published (January 1776)
children.notes: Thomas Paine's pamphlet argues for independence in plain language; sells 500,000 copies and shifts colonial public opinion decisively.
